transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2028-06-21
- Start: 15:00 PT
- Duration: 72 minutes
- Meeting ID: ff-20280621-lumen-001
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Dana (LumenWorks), Ravi, Olivia, Tom

Auto summary (optional): Walkthrough of Redwood JSON mode and Console sandbox. Showed typed outputs, error-handling / fallback orchestration. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs and VPC/on-prem constraints. Customer interested in short pilot and security paperwork.

Topics: JSON mode, schemas & guardrails; console benching; Optimize suggestions; private deployment checklist; next steps

Transcript:
[00:00:08] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE for this account. Jonah from our SE team is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:15] Dana (LumenWorks): Good, thanks. Quick note, Olivia will flag any security questions. We sent over a brief requirements doc earlier.
[00:00:23] Jonah (SE): Great, we got that. We'll use it to map the pilot. Today we'll demo JSON mode in the Console, show typed outputs and sandboxed tool invocations, plus some Optimize hints.
[00:00:36] Tom (Product): Great. Our main goal is predictable structured outputs for downstream pipelines — we can't have freeform text breaking ETL.
[00:00:44] Jonah: Totally, that's exactly where JSON mode and schema enforcement helps. We'll show an example where the model returns a typed response and the runtime enforces the contract, with fallback route if it returns invalid.
[00:00:58] Ravi: Quick infra note — we have a VPC peering requirement and use Vault for keys. Any issues with KMS or peering?
[00:01:05] Maya: No, we support customer-managed KMS and VPC peering for Private. Some teams run a Dedicated lane or private control plane. We'll cover the checklist later.
[00:01:12] Olivia (Security): Do you have SOC 2 docs and pen test reports? We need those.
[00:01:17] Maya: Yes, we'll send SOC 2 and our security pack after the call.
[00:01:22] Jonah: Ok jumping into the Console — I'm sharing my screen. Heads up, the sandbox has a JSON schema panel and a live mode where you can run tool calls in a simulated environment.
[00:01:37] [Screen share noise / brief pause] 
[00:01:45] Jonah: Here is a schema for a "medical-claim-extraction" object — required fields, types, and an enum for claim_status. I'm going to run a sample prompt hitting the hosted runtime.
[00:02:01] Speaker 1: uh-huh mm-hmm
[00:02:04] Jonah: The runtime will validate output against the schema. If it fails, we can route to a fallback model variant or invoke a cleansing tool. Watch the typed output — you'll see structured fields come back, and the Console flags any mismatches.
[00:02:22] Dana: Looks good; is the validation check happening client-side or in the runtime?
[00:02:27] Jonah: It's runtime-side, so it's enforced before your app sees the response. That avoids you having to re-validate. There's also a dry-run mode to test without invoking downstream tools.
[00:02:38] Tom: Can the runtime call our internal service for enrichment if the model is unsure?
[00:02:43] Jonah: Yes — you can configure a tool call mapping. In the sandbox we demonstrated an enrichment function that calls an internal API. In production you can wire a private endpoint or use the Actions sandbox. We also support a safe-exec policy so external calls are gated.
[00:02:58] Olivia: About the private endpoint — we require mTLS and scoped tokens. Works with your product?
[00:03:03] Jonah: We support mTLS and token scoping; for Private deployments you can use your existing Vault-backed tokens. Small note: some naming for secrets is different in our documentation, sorry if the doc earlier said "Redwood KMS" — that's actually just our sample config.
[00:03:20] [00:03:20] Maya: Quick interjection — on the Optimize side, there are three levers you asked about earlier: batching, kv cache and quantization. We call it KV cash in some older notes, eeh that's a bad transcription in docs, it's KV cache.
[00:03:35] Ravi: Ha, ok. Can you show how batching affects latency for short requests?
[00:03:40] Jonah: Sure. In the Console's Optimize tab we have simulated histograms. For small single-token-ish replies, batching can actually increase p99 latency if you wait too long for a batch to fill. We recommend latency-sensitive routes use small batch windows or dedicated instances. For throughput you enable larger batches and get better cost-per-token.
[00:03:58] Dana: How about quantization? We use LLMs for rerank and embedding; will aggressive quantization affect quality?
[00:04:05] Jonah: There's a tradeoff. Optimize suggests quantization profiles per model and per workload. We can run A/B tests — e.g., int8 for embeddings often OK, but for generation with complex syntax you might need higher precision. The Console can profile and propose a quantization recommendation.
[00:04:22] Tom: Any way to automatically fallback to a higher-precision variant when quality drops?
[00:04:27] Jonah: Yes — policies. You can set a quality monitor tied to prompt evals; when metrics drop, the router shifts to a higher-quality variant automatically. We showed a canary policy in the demo.
[00:04:38] [Crosstalk]
[00:04:40] Olivia: About audit logs — we need per-request audit trails, who invoked, tokens redacted, and retention for 1 year.
[00:04:47] Maya: We capture token-level metrics and produce audit trails; retention is configurable. For Private we can store logs in your S3/GCS. There's also an event export to SIEM.
[00:04:58] Dana: Back to schema enforcement — what happens when the model returns an unknown enum value?
[00:05:03] Jonah: The runtime rejects it and triggers the configured fallback. Options: repair output using a repair model, re-run with a stricter system prompt, or call a deterministic mapping function. You can also log metrics and surface the example to the QA dashboard.
[00:05:16] Ravi: For the pilot, we need a bench that measures p50/p95/p99, token-cost, and schema failure rate. Can you produce that out of the box?
[00:05:24] Jonah: Yes, we'll provide a benchmark harness. We'll ask you for sample prompts and traffic pattern. We can run it on our Dedicated pool or replicate on your Private cluster.
[00:05:33] [Longer demo segment omitted — SE walking through Console pages and JSON sandbox, ~20 minutes of screen walk and test runs]
[00:26:00] Jonah: ...and here's the action pipeline — if schema validation fails, the event is queued for human review while the fallback model tries a repair. The workflow is configurable per route.
[00:26:14] Dana: For human-in-the-loop, how do we surface problem cases to our ops queue?
[00:26:19] Jonah: Integrations — we can push to your ticketing system or to Slack. There's a moderation queue in the Console you can configure.
[00:26:27] Tom: Any limits around tool calling frequency? We might call an enrichment API a lot.
[00:26:31] Maya: Rate limits are configurable per-route; Dedicated can guarantee throughput. For Private you manage capacity. In hosted plans we recommend quotas and backpressure policies.
[00:26:41] Olivia: Security follow-ups: can you run a network checklist with our infra team? We want a pre-flight before pilot starts.
[00:26:49] Maya: Absolutely, we'll schedule the network/KMS checklist.
[00:26:53] Dana: Pricing — what's the best model for a 2-week pilot?
[00:26:57] Maya: We usually offer a time-boxed pilot with reduced fees for Reserved capacity or a short Dedicated reservation. We'll put numbers in the pilot scope doc.
[00:27:06] Ravi: For regression monitoring, can we attach unit prompt tests so we know if a rollout regresses structured extraction?
[00:27:11] Jonah: Yes, Redwood has prompt-eval integration: you can keep a canonical test set and we run continuous evals on model rollouts and alert on regression thresholds.
[00:27:22] [00:27:22] Olivia: we also need encryption at rest certs — is your private deployment FIPS compatible?
[00:27:28] Maya: For FIPS/HSM we have options on the Private side, we'll confirm specifics in the security pack.
[00:27:35] Tom: One last product question — can we use the Console to simulate bursts to see how fallback to cheaper model behaves?
[00:27:42] Jonah: Yes — there's a traffic simulator in the Console; you can test routing policies and fallback orchestration. We'll include a sample scenario in the bench plan.
[00:27:51] Dana: Ok sounds good. Proposed pilot: 2 weeks, run bench on your Dedicated pool then move to our Private cluster for a dry run, success criteria: schema failure < 2%, p99 < 750ms for critical route, cost < $X per 10k requests.
[00:28:08] Maya: We'll draft that scope and send today.
[00:28:11] [Wrap-up, confirmations of next steps and owners] 
[00:28:20] Maya: Recap — Maya will send the pilot scope and pricing, Jonah will send bench plan, Olivia will coordinate security checklist and provide dataset + peering details. We'll aim to start the pilot the week of 2028-06-26.
[00:28:34] Olivia: noted.
[00:28:36] Ravi: Thanks, everyone.
[00:28:38] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up.

-- End of recording --

Notes: Transcription contains some minor mis-hears ("KV cash" instead of KV cache; some speaker labels generic). Customer requested SOC2 and network preflight. Agreed pilot week-of 2028-06-26, deliverables due 2028-06-23/24.
